summary:
The choice of option (b) is well supported by the measurements. Spike 1 found no early return in 0 of 15 runs, spike 3 found a 237 ms maximum UI gap, and spike 4 found the process gone in 345 ms or less. Nothing here re-opens that choice, and C2 is still the person's decision.

The supporting work around the choice has two major defects:
- **Rig isolation.** The StallRig keeps runs apart with a unique share name, but spike 1 recorded that the SMB client allows one port per server name. That breaks the "two runs at once" material case. Narrowing the mapping pre-removal also turns it into a no-op, so a killed run's leftover mapping can block every later run.
- **Where EndStopping runs.** EndStopping is placed in the finally of the scan await, but the run continues into the post-scan volume query, where Cancel can still fire. A clock started then is never cleared and shows a false "Still waiting" line on the next scan.

There are also minor gaps:
- Two of the three architecture rules miss likely cases. The mapping rule checks only .cs files and misses `net use`. The abandon rule's `\b` misses `_scanTask`.
- The hook's default of FSA_HOOK_CANCEL_DELAY_MS=3000 makes the "Close with no prior Cancel" case impossible to express.
- The check that the line collapses after return may never be observed.
- The 1.9-3 s window ignores the progress timer's interval.
- The default run proves only that the line does not appear. Nothing asserts that the UI stays responsive during the stall.
- "Closing the window quits at once" is measured only on the loopback rig, not on a real disconnect.

Citations: the SMB-timeouts page the design cited is described accurately; it covers the old CIFS/SMB1 timers and points to a separate SMB 2.x/3.0 page. The MS-SMB2 spec calls the request-expiry timer optional, so "about a minute" rests on the rig and this machine's SessionTimeout of 60 s. The wording is hedged and switches at 90 s, which is enough.

findings.claim: The StallRig keeps runs apart with a unique share name, but every run maps the same server name (127.0.0.1). Spike 1 recorded that the Windows SMB client allows only one TCP port per server name, which contradicts the design in three ways. (a) The material case 'two rig runs at once... both runs' mappings must survive and both stalls must arm' runs against that measured limit. The second New-SmbMapping to 127.0.0.1 on another port either fails or rides the first run's connection. (b) Narrowing the pre-removal to 'the exact name this run created' makes it a no-op, because a freshly generated unique name cannot already exist. That removes the only thing that cleared a killed run's leftover mapping. A non-persistent mapping to 127.0.0.1 on a dead port then plausibly blocks every later run until sign-out. That is the opposite of the contract's 'the next run uses a new unique name'. (c) The component says the rig unmaps 'when stdin closes or on kill'. A process ended with TerminateProcess cannot clean up, and the contract's own error case admits this.
findings.evidence: Spike cancel-io-interrupts-stalled-smb-call, RIG DEVIATIONS: 'the SMB client allows one port per server name, and the fixture's pre-removal regex `fsa<8hex>` on 127.0.0.1 deletes other runs' mappings'. The spike moved to IPv6 loopback to avoid this. Design 'Rig classes extracted': 'pre-removal is narrowed to the exact name this run created'. Case 'run the stall rig / two rig runs at once / both stalls must arm' is marked material. StallRig launch error_cases: 'the next run uses a new unique name and never deletes another run's'. StallRig component: 'when stdin closes or on kill'.
findings.fix: Base isolation on the server, not the share name. Serialize rig runs with a named mutex held for the rig's lifetime. While holding it, remove any leftover rig mapping to the rig's server name; that is safe because no live rig owns one. Replace the concurrency case with two cases: 'a second run waits for the first, or fails loudly', and 'a killed run's leftover mapping does not block the next run'. Alternatively, give each run its own loopback address (127.x.y.z) and prove with one run that the client accepts it. Drop 'or on kill' from the component. To settle the question, run two StallRig instances at once on 127.0.0.1, and run one StallRig after killing a previous one.

findings.claim: EndStopping runs in the finally of the scan await, but the scan run continues after that into UnlessCancelled's post-scan volume query. That query's WaitAsync(token) at :192 exists only because the token can still fire during it. If Cancel is pressed then, OnCancel runs after EndStopping, starts _stoppingClock, and nothing clears it again. The next scan then shows 'Still waiting for the drive to answer (N s)' two seconds in, with N counted from the old cancel. That is the 'past shown as present' shape the design says cannot happen. The nullable clock is itself the flag that must be reset, so 'leaves no flag to forget to reset, so the next scan starts clean without a reset step' is false. No case would catch this, because the 'scan ends while Stopping' material case has no test.
findings.evidence: Stopping state wiring: 'The await at :145-146 calls EndStopping in its finally. UnlessCancelled (:185-198) ... untouched.' Key decision: 'Deriving from a nullable clock leaves no flag to forget to reset'. Survey C4: 'The only WaitAsync(token) (line 192) is for the post-scan volume query'.
findings.fix: Put EndStopping in a finally that wraps the whole scan run, the scan await and UnlessCancelled together, and also clear the clock where a scan starts. Alternatively, give each run its own clock captured in StartScan, and show the line only while that clock is set and the scan task is not complete, so no clock can outlive its run. To confirm the window exists, read whether CancelButton is still enabled while UnlessCancelled runs.

findings.claim: The rule 'only the rig changes the machine's SMB mappings' checks only tests/**/*.cs, but New-SmbMapping and Remove-SmbMapping are PowerShell cmdlets. The one script this design gives the rig's lifecycle to is WindowCases.ps1. That is the natural place for a 'clean up after a killed StallRig' Remove-SmbMapping, which is exactly the cross-run deletion the rule exists to stop, and a loose filter could also remove the person's real Z: mapping. The pattern also misses `net use`, which spike 3 used to map Y:, and New-SmbGlobalMapping.
findings.evidence: architecture_rules[2]: files 'tests/**/*.cs', must_not_match '\b(?:New|Remove)-SmbMapping\b'. Spike ui-keeps-pumping-through-smb-stall: 'mapped the stalled share as `net use Y:`'. Z: is the person's live mapping to \\100.109.48.75\collab.
findings.fix: Widen files to tests/**/*.cs, tests/**/*.ps1 and eng/**/*.ps1. Add the patterns '\bnet(?:\.exe)?\s+use\b', '\bNew-SmbGlobalMapping\b' and '\bWNet(?:Add|Cancel)Connection'. Keep SmbRig.cs as the only exception.

findings.claim: The rule 'Cancel does not abandon the scan thread' uses the pattern '\b[Ss]can\w*\.WaitAsync\(', which cannot match `_scanTask.WaitAsync(ct)`. An underscore counts as a word character, so there is no word boundary before the `s`. This codebase names private fields with a leading underscore (the design's own _stoppingClock), so the most likely spelling of an abandoning WaitAsync on a field (e.g. `_scanTask.WaitAsync(ct)`) passes the rule. Local names without 'scan' in them, and `Task.Run(() => Scanner.Scan(...)).WaitAsync(ct)`, pass as well. The rule depends on how things are named, not on how the code is built.
findings.evidence: architecture_rules[1] must_not_match '\b[Ss]can\w*\.WaitAsync\(' with the rationale 'An architecture rule makes crossing it fail instead of leaving it to review'.
findings.fix: Ban '\.WaitAsync\(' and 'Task\.WhenAny\(' outright in src/FsAnalyser.App/**/*.cs. Move the one legitimate volume-query WaitAsync into a small named file listed in except_files. At the least, drop the leading \b.

findings.claim: When FSA_HOOK_ARMED is set, FSA_HOOK_CANCEL_DELAY_MS defaults to 3000, so an armed run always presses Cancel. The close-escape case's second shape, 'Close with no prior Cancel', therefore cannot be expressed. Spike 4, whose env names the design adopts because they are 'proven', ran with 'FSA_HOOK_CANCEL_DELAY_MS=3000 or unset', where unset meant no Cancel. The design keeps the name and changes what it means.
findings.evidence: Hook component: 'presses Cancel at FSA_HOOK_CANCEL_DELAY_MS (default 3000)'. Case 'close the window while the wait line is shown': 'Cancel then Close, and Close with no prior Cancel'. Spike closing-window-ends-process-during-stall: 'FSA_HOOK_CANCEL_DELAY_MS=3000 or unset'.
findings.fix: Treat an unset FSA_HOOK_CANCEL_DELAY_MS as 'no Cancel', as spike 4 did, and have WindowCases.ps1 set 3000 explicitly for the wait-line case.

findings.claim: The hook logs `stopping` lines 'until the window closes or the report is written'. In --report mode, EndStopping, the report write and shutdown can all run in one dispatcher continuation, so there may be no 250 ms tick between the scan returning and the logging stopping. The assertion 'detail is `-` after the scan returns' may then hold without anything being checked. 'Cancel-to-return is recorded as a measured number' also has no stated source, because report schema 1 is unchanged.
findings.evidence: Hook component: 'until the window closes or the report is written'. Window cases, Case 1: 'detail is `-` after the scan returns... Cancel-to-return is recorded as a measured number'.
findings.fix: Have the hook write one final `stopping` line and a `returned ms=` stamp from Window.Closing or Dispatcher.ShutdownStarted. The case then asserts that this line's detail is `-` and takes Cancel-to-return from it.

findings.claim: The case's window for the first non-empty detail, 1.9 to 3 s after Cancel, has to absorb four delays: the 2 s gate, the progress timer's interval (which the design never states), the hook's 250 ms sampling, and UI jitter (spike 3 measured up to 237 ms). With a 1 s progress interval, the first detail can be observed at about 3.5 s, and the case fails while the line works.
findings.evidence: Window cases, Case 1: 'the first non-empty detail comes 1.9 to 3 s after Cancel'. Stopping state wiring: the line is updated 'On each existing progress-timer tick'. The design gives no interval for that timer.
findings.fix: Read the progress DispatcherTimer's Interval in MainWindow.xaml.cs, record it in the design, and derive the upper bound: 2 s + interval + 250 ms + 500 ms margin.

findings.claim: C-006's new assertion (every `stopping` line has detail `-`) passes unchanged if StoppingDetail is never wired, if the tick never reads the clock, or if OnCancel stops the progress timer. The boundary tests cover only the pure function. So the default run cannot tell a working line from a missing one, and the only positive check is the opt-in case, which the design assigns to validate. A later slice that stops the timer on cancel will stay green in every default run. Separately, the design depends on spike 3's invariant (the UI thread never touches the stalled share) but guards it only in StoppingWait*.cs. The opt-in case scans a UNC root rather than the mapped letter spike 3 used for the DriveInfo/PS-006 path, and it asserts no maximum gap between hook lines.
findings.evidence: Case 'cancel a scan of a stalled SMB share': 'If OnCancel stops the progress timer, the line never updates and this case fails, which is how that risk is caught'. WindowCases.ps1 -IncludeNetwork is off by default and run once at validate. Spike 3 scanned `Y:\`. architecture_rules[0] covers only StoppingWait*.cs.
findings.fix: In the opt-in wait-line case, assert that no gap between consecutive `stopping` lines exceeds 1 s from Cancel to scan return. The hook's timer runs on the UI thread, so a gap means the UI hung. Have build also run -IncludeNetwork once, with the person's consent recorded, rather than leaving it to validate alone. State in the design that the default run proves only that the line does not appear.

findings.claim: The on-screen promise 'Closing the window quits at once' shows on every stall, but spike 4 measured it only on the loopback rig, where the connection stays up and the server simply stops answering. Spike 1 showed the SMB client ignores CancelSynchronousIo on that same rig. Whether shutting down the blocked scan thread at exit completes as quickly after a Wi-Fi drop, a tunnel teardown or a sleep-resume is the same unmeasured ground as the precondition the design imports. If it does not, the window disappears but the process lingers, holding the scan data in memory. That is the 'only hides it' outcome spike 4's own falsifier names.
findings.evidence: StoppingWait wording: 'Closing the window quits at once.' Spike 4 falsifier: 'Quitting then does not end the wait. It only hides it.' Spike real-disconnect-wait-matches-rig: 'Not run: 0 of 9'. Imported precondition: 'The wait ends on its own'.
findings.fix: Add one timed Close per mode (time until the window is gone and until Get-Process no longer lists the process) to the person's 3x3 real-disconnect protocol in open_questions. Have the decision record say that the sentence rests on the rig until then.

dimensions_checked.result: M1: the rig's isolation contradicts spike 1's finding of one port per server name. m7: the close escape is unmeasured on real disconnects. Citations checked: the SMB-timeouts page the design fetched (learn.microsoft.com/en-us/archive/blogs/openspecification/cifs-and-smb-timeouts-in-windows) describes MS-CIFS/MS-SMB timers and points to a separate 'SMB 2.x and SMB 3.0 Timeouts' post. The design's statement that it does not support the 60 s SMB2 figure is accurate. MS-SMB2 'Request Expiration Timer' (learn.microsoft.com/en-us/openspecs/windows_protocols/ms-smb2/e4c02426-806d-4418-a2a6-4a8cfb522bdc) says the timer 'optionally regulates the amount of time the client waits ... before it fails the request and disconnects the connection. The client MAY<103> choose to implement this timer.' So 'about a minute' rests on the rig and this machine's SessionTimeout of 60, not on any spec guarantee. The wording is hedged ('usually'), shows elapsed time rather than a countdown, and switches at 90 s, which is proportionate. If the imported precondition is false, three outcomes are possible. If the wait is longer but still ends, the 2-90 s clause is wrong for that stall and the 90 s wording corrects it. If the wait never ends, the scan data is held until the window is closed, and the close escape is unmeasured there (m7). If the stall fails fast, the line never appears and nothing breaks. Also noted: Microsoft's alternative-ports page lists 'Admin permissions' as a prerequisite for New-SmbMapping -TcpPort, but it has been measured working unelevated on build 26200, and the measurement outranks the page.
m5: the 3 s upper bound ignores the progress timer's interval. Cancel pressed during the post-scan phase is covered in M2. Negative and boundary spans are handled in the pure function's contract.
M2: EndStopping runs before the post-scan phase ends, so a clock started after it survives into the next scan. The design's 'no flag to forget' claim is false by construction.

none: each added piece maps to a stated gap. StallRig exists because no spike's rig copy survived. The close case backs an on-screen promise. The linked pure function is there because the 90 s branch cannot be reached on the rig. The only surplus is the 'two rig runs at once' material case, which the brief does not ask for. It is folded into M1's fix.

m3: the FSA_HOOK_CANCEL_DELAY_MS default makes 'Close with no prior Cancel' impossible to express and changes the meaning of spike 4's name. m4: the post-return collapse check and the source of the Cancel-to-return figure are unspecified.

The killed-rig path is covered in M1(b)/(c): the pre-removal becomes a no-op, a leftover mapping to the same server can block later runs, and a killed process cannot unmap itself. Faulted or self-finished scans during Stopping are covered by EndStopping's finally, but it has the wrong scope (M2). A missing marker file is handled loudly.

none: the design stays inside the recorded stack (hook plus report schema 1, no App test project, xUnit only in Core.Tests, hook built outside the slnx). It says openly that it extends the hook's env contract. It recommends (b) without deciding C2, as the brief requires, and follows Q-010 for the rules file.

m1: the mapping rule checks only .cs files and misses `net use` and New-SmbGlobalMapping. m2: the abandon rule's \b fails to match underscore-prefixed fields. The pure-wording rule holds by construction, because compiling the file into Core.Tests without WPF fails on any WPF type.

m6: the default run proves only that the line does not appear. The wiring is proven only by the opt-in case at validate, and nothing asserts spike 3's UI-liveness invariant (no maximum gap check, and a UNC root instead of a mapped letter).

none: the rig is a loopback-only SMBLibrary server with a non-persistent mapping, and the hook's env vars are test-only. The risks of deleting mappings, including the person's real Z: mapping, are raised in M1 and m1. No elevation is needed or requested.
